papers.title: TDP2 couples PKA-CREB signalling to genome stability in human cerebellar development
papers.abstract: Transcription and neuronal activity in the central nervous system generate abundant DNA damage, particularly DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), rendering neural cells - and cerebellar neurons especially - vulnerable to genome instability. Tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase 2 (TDP2, also known as TTRAP) resolves topoisomerase-2-linked DSBs, and biallelic TDP2 mutations cause spinocerebellar ataxia autosomal recessive 23 (SCAR23), yet how DNA repair shapes human cerebellar development is unknown. Here we model SCAR23 in cerebellar organoids derived from patient induced pluripotent stem cells carrying TDP2 c.650del and from prime-edited isogenic TDP2 c.400C>T lines. TDP2 inactivation caused organoid hypoplasia during FGF8b-dependent cerebellar specification, which was reversed by TDP2 complementation. Single-nucleus transcriptomics across three developmental stages revealed early dysregulation of ribosome biogenesis, attenuated CREB1 regulon activity and a subsequent failure of Purkinje cell maturation. TDP2 inactivation upregulated PKIB, a cerebellum-enriched inhibitor of protein kinase A, lowering PKA and CREB phosphorylation. Whole-genome sequencing showed excess de novo deletions in mutant organoids, enriched at candidate cis-regulatory elements of neurodevelopmental genes. Pharmacological activation of the cAMP-PKA cascade restored CREB phosphorylation, reduced DNA damage and rescued organoid growth. These findings link developmental signalling to genome maintenance in the human cerebellum and identify the cAMP-PKA-CREB axis as a candidate therapeutic target in DNA-repair-deficient cerebellar disease.

papers.title: Shared-Encoder Residual Task-Bridging Network for Motor Execution to Motor Imagery EEG Transfer in Brain-Computer Interfaces
papers.abstract: Motor-imagery brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) hold promising application prospects in the fields of limb motor rehabilitation and human-computer interaction. However, the reliability of MI calibration data is limited by the difficulty of verifying participants' engagement during motor imagerywhereas motor execution (ME) provides a more readily supervised source of motor-related information.To investigate the potential of ME-derived knowledge for assisting MI decoding, we propose a Shared-Encoder Residual Task-Bridge Network (SE-RTBNet) to achieve accurate intra-subject cross-task knowledge transfer from ME to MI. The proposed framework consists of two major components: a shared encoder and a residual task-bridge module. The shared encoder extracts stable general motor representations from multi-band EEG signals and explores the shared feature patterns underlying ME and MI tasks. The residual task-bridge module is equipped with a performance-aware routing mechanism. It adaptively compensates for task-specific discrepancies between the two tasks, enabling precise cross-task feature alignment and knowledge transfer. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed model, experiments are conducted on three public datasets. The proposed method achieves average classification accuracies of 69.39%, 74.61%, and 98.94%, respectively, and outperforms existing transfer-learning algorithms in overall performance. Our model provides an effective strategy for reducing dependence on extensive MI calibration data through intra-subject cross-task knowledge transfer.The source code of the proposed SE-RTBNet is publicly available at https://github.com/Daisyzyx2002/SE-RTBNet

papers.title: Two co-occurring dynamics explain the organization of a natural movement repertoire
papers.abstract: Natural movements vary across multiple kinematic features, making it difficult to identify the dynamics shared across movements that generate a behavioral repertoire. Here, we provide a low-dimensional, interpretable generative account of the larval zebrafish hunting repertoire that links tail dynamics to behavioral outcomes. Analysis of thousands of movements spanning classically defined bout types revealed that repertoire diversity arises from continuous combinations of two simultaneously expressed dynamics: a slow, non-oscillatory bending component and a fast, oscillatory undulatory component. An analytical model captured these dynamics with six interpretable parameters and accurately reconstructed movements across the full repertoire and at two developmental stages. Different parameters predicted distinct aspects of movement outcome: maximum tail bend predicted change in heading angle, maximum tail curvature and movement duration predicted distance traveled, and oscillatory asymmetry predicted displacement direction. Relationships among the dynamical parameters constrained the movements and outcomes available to the animal. Key parameters could also be recovered directly from empirical tail kinematics, establishing them as experimentally accessible movement variables rather than model-dependent latent dimensions. Together, these results explain both the diversity and limits of a natural movement repertoire through constrained combinations of co-occurring dynamics.

papers.title: Modeling CNS inflammatory demyelination using myelin-directed CAR T cells
papers.abstract: Multiple sclerosis therapies remain confined to immunomodulatory agents that reduce inflammatory activity; none restores lost myelin, and disability can continue to accumulate independently of relapses. Development of remyelinating therapies has been hindered by models that incompletely reproduce the persistently inflamed lesions in which remyelination fails. Here we show that chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells targeting myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) build such lesions on demand. Human CD4+ CAR T cells transferred into immunodeficient mice infiltrated the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerve, producing perivascular demyelinating lesions, with reproducible optic nerve involvement. Within these discrete optic nerve lesions, treatment with the remyelinating compound clemastine reduced lesion size and improved optic nerve conduction, despite persistent inflammation. Thus, this MOG CAR T model reproduces key features of inflammatory demyelinating disease and enables testing of remyelinating therapies; more broadly, it introduces CAR T cells as programmable perturbative agents for building defined pathology in vivo.

papers.title: Biological Embedding of Social Experience Over Genomic and Neural Time Scales
papers.abstract: The "Neurons for Today, Genes for Tomorrow model" (NTGT) predicts how the brain's neural and molecular control systems interact to regulate biological embedding, whereby social experience alters the brain to shape future behavior. We report here on the first test of this model, using honey bee queen retinue pheromone (QRP) and behavioral, single-nucleus transcriptomic, and electrophysiological analyses. Consistent with theory, weaker exposure triggered a simple attraction response and transcriptomic changes primarily in the antennal lobes (AL), whereas stronger exposure induced transcriptomic changes in the mushroom bodies, a brain region affecting more complex behavior. In addition, AL electrophysiological responses to QRP were enhanced after stronger exposure, also consistent with theory. We also showed how individual differences in biological embedding can be explained by NTGT, with individual differences in brain gene regulatory network topology, especially in specific sensory cell clusters, supporting a new mechanistic framework for behavioral regulation.

papers.title: Stage-Dependent Requirement for SETX in Human Motor Neuron Maturation and Survival
papers.abstract: Senataxin (SETX) is an RNA/DNA helicase involved in transcription, RNA processing, R-loop resolution, and genome maintenance. Mutations in SETX cause neurological disorders, but its role in human motor neuron (MN) development remains unclear. Here, we examined SETX function using isogenic SETX knockout (KO) human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), shRNA-mediated knockdown, and direct conversion of fibroblasts into MNs. SETX expression increased during differentiation from hiPSCs to neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and MNs. SETX loss slowed hiPSC and NPC proliferation without preventing MN generation. However, SETX-deficient MNs developed shorter neurites, dystrophic swellings, and progressive neuronal loss. MEA recordings showed reduced firing and burst activity and almost no synchronized network bursts. RNA hybrid accumulation increased after SETX loss, with the largest relative increase in MNs among the cell types examined. RNA-seq revealed altered neurodevelopmental gene expression at the NPC stage and during MN differentiation, together with increased expression of stress- and apoptosis-associated genes. Proteomic analysis identified changes in proteins involved in neuronal structure, synaptic function, RNA regulation, and cellular homeostasis. Concordant decreases in selected RNAs and proteins supported disruption of neuronal structural and synaptic programs. Together, these findings reveal a stage-dependent requirement for SETX and identify SETX as an important regulator of transcriptional programs governing human MN maturation, function, and survival, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding the selective MN vulnerability associated with SETX-linked neurological diseases.

papers.title: Multistage gradient-based whole-cortex modeling for joint inference of regional circuit heterogeneity and interregional structural connectivity
papers.abstract: Current non-invasive neuroimaging methods cannot directly resolve regional circuit heterogeneity and interregional structural connectivity, limiting mechanistic understanding of brain structure-function relationships and accurate whole-brain modeling. Here we introduce StaGIC (Staged Gradient-based Inference of Circuitry), a method that jointly infers regional circuit heterogeneity and model-constrained structural connectivity (SC) from resting-state functional connectivity (FC) and functional connectivity dynamics (FCD). Ablation and synthetic-recovery experiments show that staged optimization improves fits to functional data and ground-truth parameter recovery, with inferred SC remaining highly consistent across retained solutions from independent optimization runs. In human data, freely optimized regional parameters exhibit consistent relationships with cortical hierarchy across parcellations, while SC inference substantially improves FC reconstruction. In macaque and marmoset data, inferred SC shows stronger correlation with tracer-derived projections than diffusion MRI estimates, particularly for long-range connections. As a proof of concept in computational psychiatry, group-level models of major depressive disorder (MDD) reproduce MDD-associated FC differences and generate exploratory hypotheses about hierarchical differentiation and interregional projection organization. StaGIC thus provides a differentiable framework for inferring multiscale cortical organization from non-invasive functional imaging.

papers.title: Beyond morphometry: Adolescent brain microarchitecture reflects sex differences in pubertal timing and hormones
papers.abstract: Puberty is a sensitive neurodevelopmental period characterized by dramatic increases in adrenal and gonadal hormones, yet how these changes relate to human brain microarchitecture remains unclear. Here, we used restriction spectrum imaging (RSI) to link peripubertal hormone levels to individual differences in brain microarchitecture (i.e., cellular and neurite density) in 7,457 youth (ages 9 to 13 years) from the ABCD Study. Sex- and age-stratified multi-task regression analyses identified microarchitecture patterns jointly associated with physical pubertal maturation and each dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), testosterone, estradiol (in female youth), in turn, combining repeated cross-validation with permutation-based feature importance. At ages 9 to 11 years, microarchitecture differences explained 11-13% of pubertal hormone variability in female youth and 4-6% in male youth. Further, microarchitecture features were differentially associated with pubertal hormones. Younger male youth exhibited widespread pubertal hormone-related differences in neurite density that consolidated into fewer, stronger associations with age, while female youth exhibited age-related expansion in pubertal cellular density differences. Anatomically, hormone-relevant microarchitecture consistently included reward processing hubs (e.g., pallidum, accumbens, orbitofrontal cortex). Because animal models suggest that DHEA and testosterone metabolites have opposing effects on GABAergic signaling, we hypothesize that future research should investigate gray matter microarchitecture for insight into pubertal hormone contributions to adolescent refinement of excitatory-inhibitory balance. Ultimately, these findings provide a starting point for investigating how pubertal endocrine changes shape reward circuitry and neurotransmitter systems, with potential implications for the pubertal emergence of sex differences in adolescent psychopathology.

papers.title: Optoretinographic measurements of cone photoreceptor function in disease-affected retinas
papers.abstract: Optoretinography (ORG) provides a noninvasive approach for measuring stimulus-evoked photoreceptor responses in the living human retina, but its application to retinal disease using clinically translatable imaging systems remains limited. Here, we applied velocity-based ORG using a clinical-grade swept-source optical coherence tomography (OCT) system to assess photoreceptor function in disease-affected human retinas and healthy controls. Following pupil dilation and dark adaptation, repeated B-scans were acquired at 400 Hz during visible-light stimulation using a phase-sensitive 100-kHz, 1060-nm swept-source OCT system. Stimulus-evoked optical path length changes between the inner segment/outer segment junction (IS/OS) and cone outer segment tips (COST) were used to quantify cone outer-segment responses. Healthy retinas exhibited rapid and reproducible responses characterized by an initial outer-segment contraction followed by elongation, whereas disease-affected retinas exhibited quantitatively reduced or altered response amplitudes and temporal dynamics. ORG also detected functional improvement following treatment in a vitamin-A-deficient retina. These findings demonstrate the ability of velocity-based ORG to quantitatively detect photoreceptor dysfunction and functional change using a clinically compatible OCT platform, supporting its potential as a noninvasive functional biomarker for retinal disease and therapeutic response.

papers.title: Probe-assisted Structural Topography Reveals In-tissue Lesion Heterogeneity in Alzheimer's Disease
papers.abstract: Disease lesions are typically defined by morphology, yet this classification often masks underlying structural heterogeneity. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) plaques appear as featureless deposits under conventional microscopy, obscuring distinct sub-regions with divergent packing, maturation, and pathological potential. Here, we present Probe-Assisted Structural Topography of Amyloid (PASTA), a single-staining framework that combines a novel pan-A{beta} probe (NapIM) with fluorescence lifetime-resolved detection and super-resolution microscopy to unmask this hidden complexity. Leveraging PASTA, we quantify plaque maturity via the Protofibril Index (PFI) at sub-lesion level, and resolve the three-dimensional (3D) in-tissue architecture of A{beta} plaques at ~30 nm resolution, identifying radially extended A{beta} branches as fundamental structural units. PASTA enables structural mapping across plaque developmental stages to reconstruct their dynamic growth trajectories, resolving two distinct assembly lineages (dense and loose) with divergent growth paths that converge to a mixed terminal subtype and share a common transition point. We further applied PASTA for mapping microglial engagement, linking interdigitated microglial contacts to dense plaque compaction and uncontacted fibril branches to loose morphology. Together, PASTA provides an unprecedented framework for understanding A{beta} heterogeneity, nanoscale architecture, and microglial-mediated remodeling in AD.

papers.title: Implication of the amyloid precursor protein expressed in GABAergic interneurons for CA3 neuronal dynamics
papers.abstract: The amyloid precursor protein (APP), a key player in Alzheimers' disease (AD, is ubiquitously expressed in a large majority of neurons, including GABAergic interneurons (INTs) in the hippocampus. INT dysfunction and subsequent abnormalities in neural circuits have emerged as potential mechanisms of cognitive decline in AD. How APP expressed in selective classes of hippocampal INTs controls local neuronal activity and thereby influences brain rhythms remains unclear. We investigated the physiological function of APP in GABAergic INTs with regard to intrinsic excitability, synaptic properties and circuit activity in the hippocampal CA3 region. We selectively deleted APP, and its homolog APLP2 to prevent compensatory mechanisms, in CA3 INTs. We categorized INTs into different clusters based on morphological and electrophysiological properties, and detected only subtle differences in intrinsic excitability and dendritic complexity between control and conditional KO INTs. In contrast, the selective deletion of APP/APLP2 in CA3 INTs impaired the amplitude and kinetics of spontaneous inhibitory currents in CA3 pyramidal cells (PCs). We further performed in vivo silicon probe recordings within CA3 in head-fixed awake mice to investigate the impact of APP/APLP2 deletion on CA3 circuit activity. By analysing oscillations and the spiking activity of putative CA3 PCs and INTs we revealed alterations in the cross-frequency coupling at oscillatory frequencies in the low gamma range, as well as in the strength of connections specifically between INTs. Our work helps better understand the physiological contribution of APP to network activity and to excitatory/inhibitory balance within hippocampal circuits, which are impaired in AD.

papers.title: Electrophysiological correlates of placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia during the anticipation and delivery of pain
papers.abstract: Positive and negative expectations can substantially shape pain and analgesic treatment outcomes, highlighting the need to elucidate neural mechanisms underlying placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia. The primary aim of this feasibility study was to assess adaptations to an established placebo-nocebo conditioning pain paradigm in the context of electroencephalography (EEG). The secondary aim was to assess EEG correlates of placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia during the anticipation and delivery of experimental heat pain in healthy volunteers. Placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia were induced in a within-subjects design in 20 young adults through verbal instructions, a conditioning procedure and (sham) transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation while EEG was recorded. Placebo and nocebo effects as well as positive and negative pain expectations were successfully established, demonstrating paradigm effectiveness. EEG results showed increased theta, alpha and beta power in the placebo compared to the control condition during pain delivery, and in the nocebo compared to the control condition during pain anticipation and delivery. Additionally, gamma-band power was increased in the nocebo compared to the placebo condition as a function of a higher perceived pain intensity. Taken together, feasibility of the EEG-compatible placebo-nocebo conditioning pain paradigm was demonstrated. Furthermore, our EEG results are in line with previous findings that, in the context of placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia, link theta-, alpha- and beta-band activity to top-down processing, and gamma-band activity to expectation-modulated sensory processing.

papers.title: A plasma proteomic atlas of rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders reveals convergent molecular signatures, neurodegenerative overlap, and a cross-disorder severity index
papers.abstract: Rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders are individually too small for well-powered biomarker studies, and each is typically studied alone. We present a harmonized plasma proteomic resource that treats them together: over 10,000 proteins measured across 27 rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders and unaffected family members, 26 of them with enough participants for differential abundance analysis, paired with standardized adaptive behaviour phenotypes and released with the full analysis pipeline. Aggregating across disorders makes shared biology visible that single-disorder studies cannot resolve. Genetically distinct disorders converge onto two proteomic clusters separated along a single dominant axis, distinguishing cytoskeletal and vesicle-trafficking proteins from metabolic and hepatic ones; the grouping is independent of gene function and of clinical classification, indicating convergence on shared downstream biology rather than gene-specific pathology. Epilepsy leaves a reproducible plasma signature detectable across disorders and largely independent of genotype, identifying candidate markers of seizure burden that are shared rather than syndrome specific. These proteomes also overlap those of adult neurodegenerative disease: most disorders are enriched against at least one signature of Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, frontotemporal dementia or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, more often inversely than concordantly, placing early-life monogenic disorders on a shared axis with late-onset degeneration. A multivariate severity index built from plasma proteins tracks adaptive communication ability in disorders held out entirely from model training and distinguishes severity among individuals who share a diagnosis rather than only separating disorders from one another. Twenty-four of the prioritised cross-disorder proteins have a recorded drug interaction, several with agents already approved for other indications. Recruitment was concentrated at single sites for a subset of disorders, and results for those disorders are reported separately and descriptively throughout. Collectively, these findings support a shift from single-gene to pathway-based, cross-disorder trial strategies that leverage convergent biomarker panels and mechanistically informed, potentially repurposed interventions.

papers.title: Depletion of LKB1 in cerebellar granule cells affects parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synaptic organization and causes progressive locomotion deficits
papers.abstract: integrates sensory and motor information and transmits signals to the muscles via motor neurons. The sole cerebellar output neurons, Purkinje cells (PCs), receive two main inputs from climbing fibers (CFs) and parallel fibers (PFs), which are the axons of granule cells (GCs). The serine/threonine kinase liver kinase B1 (LKB1) regulates GC migration; however, its role in PF synapses remains unclear. We generated a novel strain of mice with a LKB1 conditional knockout (cKO) in GCs during the postnatal period to investigate the presynaptic function of LKB1. LKB1 cKO mice exhibited progressive declines in motor coordination, whereas general locomotor activity was preserved. Morphological analysis revealed shrinkage of the cerebellar molecular layer with increased microglial density, suggesting degenerative remodeling of PF-PC synapses. Conventional electron microscopy showed a slight increase in the PF terminal area in LKB1 cKO mice, whereas three-dimensional reconstructions revealed no significant differences in bouton morphology except for an increased mitochondrial volume ratio. In contrast, the proportion of PF boutons forming multiple synapses with PC spines was higher in LKB1 cKO mice than in controls, potentially altering synaptic inputs to PCs and contributing to downstream changes in cerebellar output and reduced presynaptic occupancy at neuromuscular junctions. These findings highlight the importance of LKB1 in GCs for maintaining PF-PC synaptic remodeling and cerebellar circuit integrity, which may contribute to motor coordination.

papers.title: Neural processing of linguistic speech features and their modulation by selective attention in users of hearing aids and cochlear implants
papers.abstract: Understanding speech relies on the neural processing of acoustic and linguistic features, which can both be analyzed using Temporal Response Functions (TRFs). While both types of features have been the focus of numerous studies in typical-hearing individuals, much less is known about the neural processing of continuous speech for people with hearing loss, particularly how hearing-impaired listeners process word-level features in noisy environments, where they typically struggle. We recorded EEG from hearing aid (HA, n=29) and cochlear implant (CI, n=24) users, and an age-matched typical-hearing (TH) control group (n=29), while participants listened to audiobook segments in quiet and with a competing speaker, using their personal hearing devices (CI and HA). A hierarchical encoding framework incrementally added word onset, word frequency, and word surprisal as predictors of the EEG signal. Attentional modulation was assessed by comparing encoding scores for attended versus ignored speech. All three groups showed clear neural responses to word onset, frequency, and surprisal for speech in quiet. Surprisal tracking emerged at 400~ms in TH participants, 500~ms in HA users, and 600~ms in CI users, weakest in the CI group. All three groups exhibited attentional modulation of surprisal tracking. Word frequency yielded significant encoding gains in quiet only for TH and HI listeners, not CI users. We show for the first time that CI users exhibit significant, attention-modulated neural responses to word surprisal. More broadly, surprisal tracking was present across all hearing-impaired groups but weakest in CI users, the cohort with the greatest difficulty understanding speech in noise.

papers.title: A toolkit to identify parameter degeneracy and solution manifolds of Hodgkin-Huxley type current models
papers.abstract: Countless studies have fitted Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) type models of active currents to voltage clamp data using nonlinear least squares. Yet, little is known about the uniqueness of parameter solutions and the interdependence of HH-type model parameters. Here, we show that considerable insight can be gained from the singular value decomposition (SVD) of a matrix closely related to the objective function used in the fitting procedure. After fitting all model parameters simultaneously using synthetic data originating from a representative range of experimental cases, this reveals that a manifold of solutions is possible depending on the type of voltage clamp data available and on the selected HH-type model. In such cases, we use the SVD to determine which parameters are least identifiable. Next, we develop an SVD-based manifold tracing technique that can efficiently unveil the structure of the manifold of equivalent solutions in the parameter space of the model. Our methods also identify parameter interdependencies and their impact on joint parameter confidence regions. The most salient one consistently observed across our experimental examples was between the peak conductance and reversal potential of active HH-type current models. The SVD-based strategy presented here is expected to be generally applicable to investigate parameter degeneracy and solution manifold structure in biophysical models of single neurons. Thus, our results should prove valuable for understanding the constraints imposed by the biophysics of ion channels on single neuron computation.

papers.title: A multimodal arrayed Perturb-seq platform for dissecting microglial state dynamics and target identification
papers.abstract: Microglia are highly dynamic immune cells of the central nervous system that can adopt diverse functional states in health and disease, making them both emerging therapeutic targets and challenging systems for target identification. Here, we developed TF-iMG, a human pluripotent stem cell-derived transcription factor-induced microglia model generated by inducible expression of SPI1 and CEBPA in Cas9-expressing stem cells. TF-iMG rapidly acquired microglia-like transcriptomic, morphological, inflammatory, and phagocytic features while remaining compatible with efficient lentiviral CRISPR knockout workflows that can be completed within one week. We next established an arrayed multimodal Perturb-seq platform that integrates lentiviral CRISPR knockout, multiplexed single-cell RNA sequencing, cytokine profiling, and live-cell imaging. Single-cell analysis showed that TF-iMG recapitulates intrinsic microglial heterogeneity and captures homeostatic, activated, inflammatory, and proliferative signatures. Stimulation with IL1B and IL4 reproducibly induced distinct pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory states, respectively, providing a framework for perturbation-based interrogation of microglial state regulation. Targeting IL1B and IL4 pathway components validated the platform by attenuating expected stimulus-driven state shifts. Profiling of putative microglial regulators and Alzheimer's disease-associated genes further revealed perturbation-specific transcriptional signatures, altered state occupancy, and multimodal phenotypes spanning cytokine release, morphology, and trajectory. Together, this platform enables scalable target identification in microglia.

papers.title: PreSMA population dynamics keep the beat atop the primate audiomotor hierarchy
papers.abstract: Humans move in time with musical beats, yet how the brain builds the internal beat that guides movement is unknown. We recorded 4,719 neurons in six nodes of the audiomotor circuit while monkeys tapped in synchrony with auditory metronomes at different tempos. We found a clear functional dissociation in the temporal-frontal axis. Auditory cortex detected metronome clicks and contained local clocks that tiled each interstimulus interval, whereas parietal, striatal, and motor areas, most strongly the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA), generated movement-aligned neural sequences that rescaled with tempo. Only in preSMA did population activity formed a cone-shaped manifold that jointly encoded tempo in its height, the produced interval in its width, and the timing of each tap relative to the beat in its position along the trajectory. During timing errors, preSMA activity kept conical shape but drifted toward shorter or longer tempos, revealing a hierarchical neural clock for beat synchronization.

papers.title: Rank Deficiency in Parameter Estimation for Hodgkin-Huxley Type Current Models
papers.abstract: The Jacobians of nonlinear least squares residuals play a central role when simultaneously fitting parameters of Hodgkin--Huxley (HH) type models to ionic currents measured through voltage clamp experiments. Their rank deficiency is tied to parameter degeneracy, i.e., the ability to produce the same current response with different parameters, and the Jacobians' null spaces provide insight into the structure of the parameter degeneracy, as well as into which additional experiments can reduce or even remove it. This paper analyzes Jacobian rank structure across HH-type models used for H-, A-type, fast sodium, and delayed rectifier currents. The Jacobians are rank deficient to varying degrees, depending on experimental conditions. Analytical representations of the Jacobians' null spaces are provided. In all models, one source of rank deficiency is the multiplication of the peak conductance and state variables, such as activation and inactivation, inherent to the HH-type model structure. H-current models derived from either whole cell, or cell-attached patch recordings exhibit additional rank deficiencies, implying the local existence of manifolds of parameters that lead to the same current responses. For A-type, fast sodium, and delayed rectifier models there is no additional rank deficiency, although their Jacobians may exhibit characteristics associated with ill-conditioned parameter estimation problems. Descriptions of the null spaces of these Jacobians are used to prove that the rank deficiency can be reduced or even be removed by fixing certain parameters, or by adding additional experiments. The analytical results are illustrated numerically, using data from voltage clamp experiments described in the literature.

papers.title: Disentangling tonic and phasic dopamine in fiber photometry from single recordings to cohorts
papers.abstract: Fiber photometry signals combine fast neurotransmitter transients with slower changes in baseline. However, current pipelines separate the two before measuring either, so errors in one carry over into the other. Here we present PhotoSVI, a multi-scale statistical model that splits a recording into a slow tonic signal and discrete release events, estimated together. For each recording, PhotoSVI returns event probabilities over time, the drug effect on event rate with its uncertainty, and the time course of the tonic response, and it pools recordings across a cohort. In simulations matched to experimental recordings, PhotoSVI detected transients and recovered the shape of the tonic response more accurately than existing methods. In mouse dopamine recordings, it revealed an effect that count-based analyses largely missed: a nociceptin receptor agonist enhances the phasic response to morphine while reducing the tonic one, consistent with lower tonic dopamine relieving phasic release from autoreceptor inhibition.

papers.title: Can rat cortical cultures predict what comes next, unpredictable or learned?
papers.abstract: In humans, physiological activity recorded before an unpredictable stimulus reportedly varies slightly with what the stimulus will be, an effect termed predictive anticipatory activity. Whether reduced neural preparations show it is unknown. We re-analyzed a public dataset in which twelve dissociated rat cortical cultures on high-density multi-electrode arrays performed a hidden-source inference task (DANDI 001611: 27 experiments, 691,200 trials). Two features of the dataset limit what it can test. Each experiment replays one fixed 256-trial source sequence in all 100 sessions, so the upcoming source is unpredictable only in session 1. One stimulation volley per trial arrives on an exact 1-s clock, so every pre-stimulus window lies in the previous trial's after-effects. Two questions were fixed before a confirmatory run on held-out experiments. Q1 asked whether, in session 1, a stimulation-free 250-ms window before each trial's volley carries information about the upcoming sources beyond what trial history explains. Q2 asked whether this information grows over the 100 repetitions, as learned expectation would predict. Q1 (13 experiments, 9 cultures): decoding above a shifted-label null, {Delta}AUC +0.003, 95% CI -0.026 to +0.033, randomization p = 0.73, equivalent to zero within +/-0.059 (the human effect expressed as AUC) and narrowly within +/-0.03. Q2 (12 experiments, 8 cultures): growth {Delta}G +0.004, 95% CI -0.006 to +0.013, p = 0.29, equivalent within +/-0.02. Pre-stimulus activity thus carried no detectable information about the stimulus, and none emerged with repetition.

papers.title: Neural rosettes emerge from an interconnected tubular network in human cortical organoids
papers.abstract: Cortical organoids generate multiple neural rosettes, self-organizing and radially arranged structures that resemble ventricular zones of the developing brain. Here, we show that these rosettes, commonly considered as discrete entities, originate from an interconnected tubular network. We demonstrate that the formation of this continuous structure involves neuroepithelial folding, invagination, and internalization, resembling aspects of neural tube formation. Using fluorescently labeled polyethylene nanoplastics as extracellular tracers, we further show that they accumulate within the developing tubular lumen, consistent with its formation through neuroepithelial folding and internalization. These findings provide new insights into early human brain morphogenesis and suggest the potential utility of cortical organoids for investigating developmental processes relevant to neural tube defects.

papers.title: Within-Subject Precision Measurement: Theory and Utility of Assessing Change Scores and Their Variance
papers.abstract: Within-subject studies gain statistical power by removing stable between-subject differences from the comparison. However, the metrics commonly used to select measurement instruments and anticipate their within-subject performance are often based on between-subject correlations of raw scores from test-retest designs. Measuring each subject's change directly -- after an intervention, and ideally more than once -- provides a firmer basis for evaluating measurement precision and planning studies of within-subject change. Here we describe the statistical theory behind estimating measurement properties from change scores. In one instantiation, the pre- and post-intervention measurements are each made twice, yielding the duplicate change-score design. Such a design provides an estimate of the mean signal change and enables the decomposition of the total observed variance of change scores into true between-subject response heterogeneity and measurement noise. In extended designs, where multiple measures are collected within and across days, measurement noise can be further decomposed to distinguish within-session from between-day measurement variability. These estimates supply the inputs needed for within-subject study design, including providing a basis for selecting among alternative measurements and comparing processing pipelines, performing power calculations, and estimating the precision limits of detecting change within individual subjects.

papers.title: Endothelial VCAM1 links oncogenic KRAS signaling to myeloid inflammation and hemorrhagic instability in brain arteriovenous malformations
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic conversion is the most devastating complication of brain arteriovenous malformations (bAVMs). However, endothelial mechanisms promoting macrophages (M{varphi}) recruitment, microglia (MG) activation, and bAVM lesion instability remain unclear. We investigated vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM1) as a mediator linking oncogenic endothelial signaling to myeloid cell responses and hemorrhagic progression in bAVMs. METHODS: We performed integrated transcriptomic analysis of human bAVM and epilepsy-control brain tissues, with validation in local bAVM specimens. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of bAVM lesions and intact brain tissues from mutant KRAS-induced bAVM mice were followed by histological validation. Using AAV-BR1-KRASG12V-injected Cx3cr1-gfp;Ccr2-rfp mice, we performed intravital imaging to assess M{varphi}/MG responses to VCAM1 neutralization. Hemorrhage and myeloid cell responses were also evaluated following endothelial-specific VCAM1 deletion. Plasma soluble VCAM1 (sVCAM1) was measured in patients with unruptured and ruptured bAVMs and unruptured aneurysm controls. Effects of sVCAM1 on MG activation were examined in vitro. RESULTS: Integrated human endothelial bulk and single-cell RNA-sequencing and tissue validation identified VCAM1 upregulation in bAVMs, including unruptured lesions. Plasma analyses showed increased sVCAM1 in unruptured and ruptured bAVM patients compared with unruptured aneurysm controls. In mutant KRAS-induced bAVM mice, transcriptomic and proteomic analyses demonstrated increased VCAM1 expression, with endothelial localization confirmed histologically. In vitro, mutant KRAS increased sVCAM1 production, while recombinant sVCAM1 stimulated inflammatory mediator expression in MG. Both MG and M{varphi} expressed VLA-4, a major VCAM1 receptor. Intravital imaging showed that VCAM1 neutralization reduced M{varphi} accumulation and MG activation, while early VCAM1 neutralization reduced hemorrhagic burden. Consistently, endothelial-specific VCAM1 deletion reduced M{varphi} accumulation, MG activation, and hemorrhage volume in bAVM mice and improved behavioral performance. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify endothelial VCAM1 as an upstream mediator linking mutant KRAS signaling to myeloid cell responses and hemorrhagic progression in bAVMs. This study establishes endothelial VCAM1 as a potential therapeutic target for attenuating hemorrhagic progression.

papers.title: Developmental emergence of cue-specific fear memory parallels maturation of prefrontal-amygdala circuitry in mice
papers.abstract: Fear memories formed in early life are forgotten rapidly, but the circuits that delay stable memory expression are not well defined. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) projects to the basolateral amygdala (BLA), and both regions mature late, yet the behavior, anatomy and physiology of this pathway have rarely been examined together across development. We trained mice in cued auditory fear conditioning at postnatal day (P) 14-15, P20-21 or P59-70 and tested tone-evoked freezing 1, 7 and 14 days later. Early juvenile mice showed no cue-specific freezing at any memory retrieval time points, late juvenile mice showed it at 7 and 14 days but not at 1 day, and adults showed it at all retrieval time points. In separate mice, mPFC axons were low in the BLA at P11 and more abundant at P38 and P90, and light-evoked prelimbic synaptic responses in BLA principal neurons were not detectable at P11 but were robust at P35 and P70. Spontaneous synaptic currents and intrinsic excitability of BLA principal neurons, and excitability of prelimbic principal neurons and interneurons, also changed between P11 and adulthood. These data identify a protracted period of mPFC-BLA circuit maturation that overlaps the emergence of cue-specific fear and define the ages at which candidate mechanisms can be tested.

papers.title: Transcriptomic and Lipidomic Profiling of Human iPSC-Derived Microglia Reveals TREM2-Dependent and -Independent Processes
papers.abstract: TREM2 has been implicated in AD as a critical regulator of microglial functions and loss of function mutations in TREM2 increases one's risk of developing AD. Given the diverse functional roles of TREM2, we sought to unravel how it affects downstream pathways using human iPSC-derived microglia-like cells (iMGLs) derived from TREM2 knockout (KO) and isogenic control lines and assessing the response to oligomeric amyloid-{beta} 42 (oA{beta}42). While previous studies have primarily used fibrillar A{beta}, we focused on microglial responses to oA{beta}42 given their disease relevance and potent cytotoxic effects. At baseline, we identified a set of TREM2-dependent genes, which corresponded to the DAM signature in mice and disease-associated signatures in humans. Additionally, loss of TREM2 resulted in increased expression of cholesterol biosynthesis genes. In response to oA{beta}42, we found that the transcriptional response was largely TREM2-independent and corresponded to a strong induction of inflammatory pathways, with TREM2 also being downregulated in control iMGLs. We identified subsets of genes and pathways that were unique to either control, such as mitochondrial DNA and RNA degradation, or TREM2 KO iMGLs, such as the senescence-associated secretory pathway and adipogenesis, suggesting some differences in gene expression driven by TREM2 in response to oA{beta}42. Given that the inflammatory response was TREM2-independent, we sought to identify signaling pathways that contributed to inflammation. Inhibition of toll-like receptor signaling significantly reduced the expression of pro-inflammatory genes and modestly increased expression of TREM2 and TREM2-dependent genes. Consistent with our transcriptional data, cytokine production and secretion in response to oA{beta}42 was significantly increased to similar levels in both controls and TREM2 KO iMGLs. Lipidomic profiling of microglia revealed that triglycerides and lactosylceramides were significantly increased in both control and TREM2 KO iMGLs in response to oA{beta}42. TREM2 KO iMGLs had decreased levels of BMPs and increased levels of cholesterol esters across all conditions, further highlighting a role for TREM2 in maintaining lipid homeostasis in microglia. Taken together, we describe genes, pathways, and lipids that are associated with TREM2 expression that likely influence microglial responses to oA{beta}42.

papers.title: Long-lasting chromatin and transcriptional states shape the maintenance of memory ensembles
papers.abstract: Memories of recent events are stored within minutes in neuronal ensembles in the hippocampus. Over days to weeks, these memories undergo consolidation, and later retrieval depends on reactivation of a subset of neurons within the ensemble. However, how transient experiences produce lasting molecular and cellular changes in hippocampal ensemble neurons remains unknown. Here, we profile the functional, transcriptional, and gene regulatory states of hippocampal memory ensemble neurons at single cell resolution across multiple remote timepoints following single trial contextual fear conditioning. We uncover long lasting, cell type specific chromatin and gene expression changes after learning that coincide with sustained shifts in synaptic plasticity. Within dentate gyrus granule ensembles, we identify a persistent chromatin transcriptional program that emerges in a subset of ensemble neurons and is marked by sustained expression of many synaptic genes. This transcriptional signature predicts which neurons will be reactivated during memory recall, suggesting that only a fraction of initial ensemble neurons maintains a molecular state supporting later reactivation. Regulatory elements associated with this persistent state are highly enriched for AP1 motifs, the cognate binding sites for Fos family transcription factors, even though FOS protein has long since decayed away. Instead, we detect long lasting FOSB binding at these elements, suggesting a mechanism by which the effects of immediate early gene driven transcription are extended beyond the initial induction window. FOSB is particularly enriched in ensemble neurons that maintain enduring gene expression changes, suggesting it sustains chromatin accessibility and prolonged transcription in neurons reactivatable during memory retrieval. Together, these findings identify molecular mechanisms underlying the maintenance, maturation, and evolution of hippocampal memory ensembles over time.

papers.title: Pathogenic human autoantibodies target the soluble CASPR2 ectodomain to induce network hyperexcitability
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which autoantibodies contribute to antibody-mediated neurological diseases remain poorly understood. Autoantibodies targeting the extracellular domain of CASPR2 are found in patients with clinical features consistent with hyperexcitability, including neuromyotonia and seizures. These antibodies are reported to disrupt the functions of membrane-embedded CASPR2. However, given that CASPR2 is also detected in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which contains CASPR2 autoantibodies, targeting of CSF-shed CASPR2 may represent an additional pathogenic mechanism, introducing a novel paradigm of soluble antigen modulation by autoantibodies. Here, we found that patient-derived polyclonal and monoclonal CASPR2 antibodies enhanced neuronal network excitability and selectively amplified excitatory synaptic transmission in human and rat primary cortical neurons. In addition, CASPR2 antibodies impaired calcium homeostasis and altered the intrinsic properties of both excitatory and inhibitory neurons. Notably, these antibodies depleted CASPR2 from both neuronal culture medium and patient CSF, suggesting targeting of the shed CASPR2 ectodomain. Knockdown of plasma membrane calcium ATPase 2 (PMCA2), a reported target of the CASPR2 ectodomain, abrogated the observed effects of CASPR2 antibodies. Together, our findings identify shed CASPR2 as a underrecognized pathogenic target of CASPR2 autoantibodies and demonstrate that its neutralization disrupts PMCA2-mediated calcium regulation, driving neuronal network hyperexcitability. More broadly, we identify the neuronal sheddome as a source of autoantibody targets and soluble protein neutralization as a novel disease mechanism, highlighting shed CASPR2 as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target.

papers.title: Human Endogenous Retrovirus K RNA triggers cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregation by initiating pathological nuclear condensates
papers.abstract: Cytoplasmic aggregation of the nuclear RNA-binding protein TDP-43 is a defining pathology of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and is seen in many cases of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet what initiates this process remains unknown. Here we identify an unexpected trigger: RNA from human endogenous retrovirus-K (HERV-K), an ancient retroviral element embedded in the human genome. Using CRISPR-engineered cells expressing Halo-tagged TDP-43 at endogenous levels, we show that HERV-K activation drives formation of cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregates and functional loss of nuclear TDP-43, measured by aberrant cryptic exon inclusion. Surprisingly, cytoplasmic aggregation is preceded by the appearance of phosphorylated TDP-43 condensates in the nucleus, structures we term Pathological ERV-TDP-43-Associated Nuclear Spheres (PETANS). Live-cell imaging reveals that cytoplasmic inclusions originate directly from these nuclear bodies. This inverts the conventional model to suggest that pathological TDP-43 condensation begins in the nucleus, not the cytoplasm. Super-resolution imaging and structure-function mapping show that HERV-K RNA localizes within PETANS and drives their formation, with a minimal UG-rich non-coding element sufficient to induce the full cascade of nuclear and cytoplasmic pathology. Our findings establish an endogenous retroviral RNA as a direct molecular nucleator of TDP-43 proteinopathy.

papers.title: Gene expression in the hypothalamus of gonad-sex chromosome divergent embryonic chickens
papers.abstract: Sexual differentiation of the brain of birds is shaped by gonadal steroid hormones and also by cell-autonomous mechanisms resulting from limited sex chromosome dosage compensation. In this study, we compare gene expression in the hypothalamus of gonad-sex chromosome divergent embryonic chickens treated with the aromatase inhibitor fadrozole to their control counterparts. Consistent with a lack of dosage compensation, we find a robust effect of sex chromosomes on hypothalamic gene expression, and a large portion of differentially expressed genes were on the Z and W sex chromosomes. Despite the presence of developing testes and markedly reduced estrogen concentrations in fadrozole-treated chromosomal female (ZW) birds, we find modest effects of gonadal hormones on gene expression in the brain. Weighted gene coexpression network analysis revealed that the most prominent effects were attributable to interactions between chromosomal sex and treatment. Our results highlight that chromosomal sex and steroid hormones together shape the sexual differentiation of the embryonic avian brain, challenging the primacy of the organizational effects of sex steroids on the brain during development.
